terms.definition: EC2 pricing model with no upfront payment or long-term commitment — you pay by the hour or second for what you use.
terms.example: Like renting a car by the day — maximum flexibility, but not the cheapest if you need it long-term.

terms.definition: A commitment to use a specific EC2 or database instance for 1 or 3 years in exchange for up to 72% discount over On-Demand pricing.
terms.example: Like signing a yearly apartment lease — you commit for a year, but pay significantly less per month than a hotel.

terms.definition: EC2 instances that use AWS's spare capacity at discounts of up to 90% — but can be reclaimed by AWS with 2 minutes' notice.
terms.example: Like standby airline seats — great price, but you might get bumped if a paying passenger needs the seat.

terms.definition: A flexible commitment model where you commit to a consistent dollar-per-hour of compute usage in exchange for discounts on EC2, Fargate, and Lambda.
terms.example: Like a monthly gym membership with a class credit — the credit applies to any classes (EC2, Lambda, Fargate), not just one type.

terms.definition: An entire physical AWS server reserved exclusively for your use — the most expensive EC2 option, typically used for software licensing compliance.
terms.example: Like renting an entire apartment building rather than one unit — expensive, but necessary if your lease requires a specific address.

terms.definition: An EC2 instance that runs on hardware dedicated to your account, but AWS can move it between physical servers as needed — less expensive than a Dedicated Host.
terms.example: Like having a private room in a hotel — no roommates, but the hotel can still move you to a different room.

terms.definition: The practice of selecting the smallest EC2 instance type that meets actual workload requirements, based on CloudWatch utilization metrics rather than guessing.
terms.example: Like buying a car that fits your family — not a bus, not a motorcycle. Match the tool to the actual need.

terms.definition: A free web tool at calculator.aws that estimates AWS costs for proposed architectures — no AWS account required.
terms.example: Like using a mortgage calculator before buying a house — estimates costs so you can plan before committing.

terms.definition: A free built-in AWS Console tool that visualizes historical and current spending, filterable by service, region, and account.
terms.example: Like your bank's spending summary that shows where your money went last month, broken down by category.

terms.definition: A free AWS service that continuously analyzes your account and provides recommendations across Cost Optimization, Security, Performance, Fault Tolerance, and Service Limits.
terms.example: Like having a financial advisor review your account and say 'you're paying for a gym membership you haven't used in 3 months.'

terms.definition: Different tiers of Amazon S3 storage with varying costs and retrieval speeds — from Standard (instant, expensive) to Glacier Deep Archive (hours retrieval, cheapest).
terms.example: Like different storage units — a climate-controlled unit near downtown costs more but is easy to access; a remote warehouse is dirt cheap but takes effort to retrieve anything.

terms.definition: An automated rule that transitions S3 objects between storage classes (or deletes them) based on age or last-access patterns.
terms.example: Like telling your filing system: 'If a document is older than 6 months, move it to the archive room. If older than 7 years, shred it.'

terms.definition: The lowest-cost S3 storage class, using tape drives, with retrieval times of several hours — designed for data that must be retained but is almost never accessed.
terms.example: Like a bank vault for safety deposit boxes — extremely secure and cheap to maintain, but you can't walk in and grab something immediately.

terms.definition: The movement of data from AWS to the public internet or between AWS regions — one of the three fundamental cost drivers, typically charged by GB.
terms.example: Like a restaurant charging you when food leaves the kitchen — bringing ingredients in is free, but serving customers has a cost.

terms.definition: Large upfront investment in physical assets like servers and data centers — the traditional on-premises IT model that cloud computing replaces with OpEx.
terms.example: Like buying vs. renting a building — CapEx is buying (big upfront cost, yours forever), OpEx is renting (pay as you go).

terms.definition: Pay-as-you-go spending for services consumed — the AWS model that replaces large upfront CapEx investments with variable costs aligned to usage.
terms.example: Like paying a monthly electricity bill instead of buying a power plant.

terms.definition: AWS's set of best practices and design principles organized into six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability.
terms.example: Like a building code for cloud architecture — a checklist of principles that ensure your system is built on solid foundations.

terms.definition: One of the six pillars of the Well-Architected Framework — focused on running systems at the lowest price point while still delivering required business value.
terms.example: Like a financial audit for your cloud infrastructure — regularly reviewing and optimizing spending without sacrificing what matters.

terms.definition: An AWS feature that automatically adds or removes EC2 instances based on demand, ensuring you pay for capacity only when you need it.
terms.example: Like a coffee shop that calls in extra baristas on Monday mornings and sends them home on slow afternoons — staff matches demand.

terms.definition: A set of AWS service limits available at no charge — some for 12 months after account creation, others always-free up to certain usage thresholds.
terms.example: Like a freemium software plan — use the basic features for free indefinitely, pay only when you need more capacity or features.

terms.definition: An S3 storage class that automatically moves objects between frequent and infrequent access tiers based on actual access patterns, with no retrieval fees.
terms.example: Like a smart closet organizer that moves clothes you wear often to the front and rarely worn items to the back — automatically, without you doing anything.

terms.definition: Different categories of Amazon EBS storage (gp3, io2, st1, sc1) optimized for different workloads — SSD for low latency, HDD for throughput or cold storage.
terms.example: Like choosing between a sports car (fast, expensive SSD) or a cargo truck (slower but cheap HDD) depending on whether you need speed or volume.
